prompt: What does the compiler say about `val course: String = null`?
hint: `String` without a question mark.

choices.why: An empty string is `""`, a value; `null` is the absence of one, and a `String` refuses it.

choices.text: It refuses: null cannot be a value of a non-null type
choices.why: Right: `null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String'`, and no jar is written.

choices.text: It compiles, and the program crashes when it reaches that line
choices.why: The refusal is at compile time; this program never runs.
A written type is checked, never replaced by another.

prompt: `val note: String? = "read chapter 3"` and then `println(note.length)`. Why does the compiler refuse, when the note is plainly there?
hint: What is a type a promise about?

choices.text: Because a string literal is stored as `null` until first used
choices.why: The literal is a value from the start; nothing is lazy here.

choices.text: `length` is not defined on strings that came from a literal
choices.why: Every `String` has `length`; the trouble is the `?`.

choices.text: The type says it could be null, and a type covers every value it allows
choices.why: Right: the compiler reasons from `String?`, not from this particular value.

choices.text: Smart casts do not work on literals
choices.why: No check was written, so there was nothing to smart cast from.

prompt: `name` is a `String`. Which line compiles with nothing else written?

prompt: `note` is a `String?`. What is the type of `note?.length`?
hint: One of its two outcomes is `null`.

choices.why: It can be `null`, so it cannot be `Int`.
Right: a safe call is always nullable.
`length` is a number; the `?` is what the safe call adds.
`Nothing?` holds only `null`, and this holds lengths too.

prompt: `SafeCall.kt` printed `14`, `null` and `0` for its three notes. What does the `0` tell you?
hint: Look at the third item of the list.

choices.text: That `?.` turns a missing note into a length of zero
choices.why: The missing note printed `null`; `?.` never invents a value.

choices.text: That the third note is an empty string, which is present
choices.why: Right: `""` is a string of length 0, and only `null` is absent.

choices.text: That the list had a third element the program could not read
choices.why: An unreadable element would not print anything as tidy as `0`; the element was `""`.
The loop printed lengths, not positions.

prompt: `second` is `null`. In `second?.uppercase()?.length`, how many functions actually run?
hint: A chain stops at the first null.

choices.why: `uppercase` is never called on `null`; the first `?.` short-circuits.
`uppercase` would need a string to run on, and there is none.

choices.text: None: the chain gives `null` at the first `?.`
choices.why: Right: nothing after the first missing value runs.
A safe call never throws for a `null`; it hands back `null`.

choices.why: The null case left the function, so it cannot reach the next line.

prompt: In `SmartCast.kt`, why does `note.length` compile on the last line of `describe`?
hint: What happened when `note` was `null`?

choices.why: It declares `String?`; the check made it a `String` from there on.

choices.text: Because a null `note` has already returned
choices.why: Right: past the early return, only a present note can arrive.

choices.text: Because string templates accept nullable values
choices.why: Printing a null is fine, but `.length` is a call on it, which is what needs the cast.

choices.text: Because the call site passes a literal
choices.why: The function is compiled once, for every caller, including `describe(null)`.

prompt: Why is `draft.note.length` refused after `if (draft.note != null)`, when `note` is a `var` property?
hint: The message says what could happen in between.

choices.text: Something else could set the property to `null` between the check and the use
choices.why: Right: the check proves nothing about a value that can change, so take a `val` copy.

choices.text: Smart casts work on parameters and never on objects
choices.why: They work on a `val` property of an object in the same module; it is the `var` that stops it.

choices.text: The class was declared in the same file
choices.why: Being in the same file helps; it is not the obstacle.

choices.text: `!=` compares identity, so the check is unreliable
choices.why: `!= null` is a plain null check, and it is reliable at the moment it runs.

prompt: What does `?: error("minutes must be a number, got '$input'")` give you that `!!` does not?
hint: Both stop the program.

choices.why: `error` throws `IllegalStateException`, so the program stops as well.

choices.text: A message saying what was expected and what arrived
choices.why: Right: the person reading the log learns the input was `forty`.

choices.text: A line number in the stack trace, pointing at the failing call
choices.why: `!!` gave a line number too: `Bang.kt:4`.
Both are a handful of bytes of bytecode.

prompt: Section 06 names a few honest uses of `!!`. Which of these are among them? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Yes: a crash with a line number is the failure a test wants.

choices.text: Reading a value a user typed into a form

choices.text: A program you will throw away

prompt: `val home = System.getenv("STUDY_HOME")` and then `home.length`. Why did that compile?
hint: Where does `getenv` come from?

choices.text: Because environment variables are never null on Linux
choices.why: The second run showed the opposite: unset gives `null`.
No type was written; it was inferred.

choices.text: `getenv` is Java, and `home` got a platform type
choices.why: Right: a `String!` is allowed either way, and fails like Java.

choices.text: Because `length` is a safe property on strings
choices.why: No property is safe on a null; the platform type is why the compiler allowed it.

prompt: `val home: String = System.getenv("STUDY_HOME")` with the variable unset. Where does the program fail?
hint: Kotlin inserts something at that line.

choices.text: It does not compile, because `getenv` can return null
choices.why: A platform type may be declared either way, so it compiles.

choices.text: At that very line, with `getenv(...) must not be null`
choices.why: Right: the inserted check fails at the border.

choices.text: At the first line that uses `home`
choices.why: That is the undeclared platform type; declaring `String` moves the failure to the border.
Kotlin never turns `null` into `""` for you.

prompt: Which habit does section 07 recommend for every value that comes from Java?
hint: Decide at the border.

choices.text: Add `!!` so a null fails early
choices.why: That turns the border into a crash without a sentence.

choices.text: Leave it inferred, exactly as you would with a Kotlin value
choices.why: Inference gives the platform type, which is the unchecked one.
Catching the crash is not the same as making absence part of the type.

choices.text: Give it a type, nullable unless documented otherwise
choices.why: Right: then the compiler is back in charge.
